To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a simple relationship exists between the extent of the LNAPII body and the emission to groundwater.
the lateral extent of LNAPL in the capillary fringes can be used as an indicator for the emissions of contaminants from the LNAPL source zone.

the relationship between the emission rate from a LNAPL source zone and the lateral extent of that source is linear and that the parameters describing this relationship are linear functions of the flow velocity and the infiltration rate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the estimation of source-zone emission at LNAPL-contaminated sites.
a practical approach to estimate the source-zone emissions from a LNAPL contaminated site.

the development of a simple method that can be used to estimate the source-zone emissions at a LNAPL contaminated site, and the relationship between the emission of contaminants and the lateral extent of LNAPL in the capillary zone.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the lateral extent of a LNAPL body is a good surrogate for the emission rate of contaminants to groundwater.
the relationship between the extent of LNAPL in the capillary zone and the emissions of contaminants from the capillary zone is linear.
a pragmatic approach for estimation and prediction of the source-zone emissions at an LNAPL contaminated site can be developed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a linear relationship between lateral extent of LNAPL body, groundwater velocity and infiltration rate can be used to predict contaminant emissions at a LNAPL contaminated site.

a simple, linear relationship between the lateral extension of the LNAPLS in the capillary zone and the contaminant emissions to the aqueous-phase is demonstrated, and that the parameters of this linear relationship are linear functions of the vertical infiltration rate and the groundwater flow velocity.
the emission of contaminants into groundwater from an LNAPL source zone is linearly dependent on the lateral extent of that zone.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, at a given site, a simple linear relationship can exist between the lateral extent (i.e., the width of the LNAPLN body in the capillarity fringe) and the emission of LNAPL contaminants to the groundwater.
, at least at a qualitative level, a simple approach can be used for the estimation of source-zone emission rates.
a site-specific linear correlation exists between the lateral spread of the LNAPLA body in the capillarity zone and the contaminant emissions from the source zone.
